bill.title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Rubber Tire Manufacturing".
bill.officialSummary: This joint resolution removes emission regulations on hazardous air pollutants under the rubber tire manufacturing source category, specifically from the rubber processing subcategory. The joint resolution nullifies the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) rule titled National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Rubber Tire Manufacturing , which addresses the decision in Louisiana Environmental Action Network v. EPA (D.C. Cir. 2020) that requires the EPA to address unregulated emissions from a major source category when it conducts the 8-year technology review. The rule implemented emissions standards for the rubber processing subcategory.

classification.plainSummary: This resolution would block an Environmental Protection Agency rule that sets limits on hazardous air pollution from rubber tire manufacturing facilities. The EPA rule was issued in response to a 2020 court decision requiring the agency to regulate emissions from the rubber processing part of tire production during its regular technology review. If passed, the resolution would nullify those emission standards and leave that subcategory unregulated.

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects rubber tire manufacturers by removing emission standards that would otherwise apply to their production facilities.
Tire manufacturers supply the transportation sector, and regulatory costs or compliance requirements could indirectly affect tire pricing and availability.

plain.whatItDoes: This joint resolution would remove emission regulations on hazardous air pollutants under the rubber tire manufacturing source category, specifically from the rubber processing subcategory.
plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who drives. People living near a road, a plant or a port.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in driving, and what a car must have. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
